title: PostgreSQL: ACID & isolation levels
description: Atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability in practice, plus the three isolation levels PostgreSQL really implements.
source: Study notes: when and how to use PostgreSQL in system design interviews

questions.prompt: A transfer debits one account and credits another inside a transaction, and the server crashes between the two statements. What happens?

options.text: The whole transaction is rolled back; neither account changes.
options.why: Right: atomicity is all or nothing.

options.text: The debit stays and the credit is retried later automatically.
options.why: Partial results are exactly what atomicity prevents.

options.text: The credit is applied and the debit is skipped.
options.why: Neither half is applied on its own.

options.text: The database keeps both accounts locked until an admin intervenes.
options.why: Crash recovery rolls back the incomplete transaction automatically.

questions.explanation: Atomicity prevents partial failures, which are hard to repair in distributed systems.

questions.prompt: A CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint exists and a transaction would make a balance negative. What does PostgreSQL do?

options.text: Rejects the statement and the transaction cannot commit as is.
options.why: Right: constraints keep the database in a valid state.

options.text: Commits the change and records a warning in the log.
options.why: Constraint violations are errors, not warnings.

options.text: Clamps the balance to zero silently and commits.
options.why: The database never rewrites your values to satisfy a constraint.

options.text: Asks the application to confirm before committing.
options.why: There is no confirmation step; the violation is an error.

questions.explanation: In ACID, consistency means rules and constraints always hold. Many NoSQL stores leave this to application code.

questions.prompt: True or false: "consistency" in ACID and "consistency" in the CAP theorem mean the same thing.

options.text: True
options.why: They are easy to confuse but differ.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: they are different ideas that share a name.

questions.explanation: ACID consistency means the data follows all constraints and rules; CAP consistency means every read sees the most recent write across nodes.

questions.prompt: What is PostgreSQL's default isolation level?

options.text: Read Committed, which sees only data committed before each query began.
options.why: Right: that is the default.

options.text: Serializable, which runs every transaction as if one at a time.
options.why: That is the strictest level and must be requested.

options.text: Read Uncommitted, which can see other transactions' unfinished work.
options.why: PostgreSQL never allows dirty reads; it treats this as Read Committed.

options.text: Repeatable Read, which freezes a snapshot per transaction.
options.why: That is available but not the default.

questions.explanation: Each query in a Read Committed transaction can see newly committed data, so repeated reads may differ.

questions.prompt: How is PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read stronger than the SQL standard requires?

options.text: It also prevents phantom reads, not just non-repeatable reads.
options.why: Right: the snapshot hides rows that others commit meanwhile.

options.text: It prevents every possible concurrency anomaly, including serialization anomalies.
options.why: Only Serializable does that; write skew can still occur.

options.text: It lets transactions see uncommitted changes for speed.
options.why: Dirty reads are never possible in PostgreSQL.

options.text: It automatically retries any transaction that conflicts.
options.why: Retries are the application's job, mostly at Serializable.

questions.explanation: Because of snapshots, you may not need Serializable where other databases would require it.

questions.prompt: What must your application be ready to do when using SERIALIZABLE isolation?

options.text: Retry transactions that the database aborts because of conflicts.
options.why: Right: serialization failures are expected under contention.

options.text: Manually lock every table before each transaction in a typical production setup.
options.why: Serializable exists so you need not reason about locks.

options.text: Disable replication so that snapshots stay consistent without any extra configuration.
options.why: Replication is unrelated to the isolation level.

options.text: Split every transaction into one statement each.
options.why: Multi-statement transactions are exactly its use case.

questions.explanation: Serializable trades concurrency for simplicity: correct results, but occasional aborts that need retry logic.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, what happens if you ask for READ UNCOMMITTED?

options.text: You get Read Committed behavior, so dirty reads cannot happen.
options.why: Right: MVCC makes dirty reads impossible at every level.

options.text: You can read other transactions' uncommitted changes for most everyday workloads.
options.why: That is true in some databases, not PostgreSQL.

options.text: The statement fails because the level is unsupported under normal operating conditions.
options.why: It is accepted but mapped to Read Committed.

options.text: You get Serializable behavior to be safe.
options.why: It maps to the weaker Read Committed, not Serializable.

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL implements three distinct behaviors although the standard names four levels.

questions.prompt: What makes a committed PostgreSQL transaction durable across a crash?

options.text: Its WAL records are flushed to disk at commit and can be replayed.
options.why: Right: the log is durable even if data pages are not yet.

options.text: Every changed data page is written to disk before the commit returns.
options.why: Data pages are written later in the background.

options.text: The replica always holds a second copy before commit returns.
options.why: Only with synchronous replication, and that is a separate setting.

options.text: The operating system cache is never used for database files.
options.why: The cache is used; durability comes from flushing the WAL.

questions.explanation: Write-ahead logging is why commits are durable yet cheap. Setting synchronous_commit = off relaxes it for speed and risks losing recent commits.

seriesDescription: Everything to know about PostgreSQL for system design interviews: when to pick it, SQL and ACID basics, indexing, scaling writes, replication and concurrency control, in eight short quizzes.
